_comment: Permission safety rails shipped by workbench-core and merged into
Rules are evaluated deny → ask → allow, before the auto-mode classifier, in
every permission mode including bypassPermissions. That is the point: a
boundary stated only in conversation is lost when context is compacted, but
HEADLESS CONSTRAINT — read before adding to `ask`:
An ask rule always forces a prompt, and a `claude -p` run has nobody to
prompt, so the call is blocked instead. workbench-dev-team dispatches Watson
unattended via `nohup claude -p --agent`, and Watson pushes branches, commits,
and opens PRs. So `Bash(git push:*)`, `Bash(git commit:*)`, and
`Bash(gh pr create:*)` are deliberately NOT in `ask` — putting them there
would kill the pipeline silently. The git-commit approval gate stays a
PreToolUse hook, which can carry a pipeline exemption; an ask rule cannot.

deny.why: Nothing the agent does should need root.
Raw block-device writes destroy disks with no undo.
Filesystem creation over an existing volume.
Rewrites remote history. Prefix matching means this also blocks `--force-with-lease` — accepted tradeoff.
Destroys the reflog, which is the undo rope for every other git mistake.
Bulk credential dump. Scoped find/add/delete are handled by ask rules instead, since plugin setup skills use them.
Private keys. A Read deny also blocks Edit on the same paths.

Application secrets at any depth. Note the cost: a Read deny also blocks Edit, so a broken .env can be neither read nor repaired. Variants like .env.local and .env.production are NOT covered — a `**/.env.*` rule would also catch .env.example, which holds no secrets and is read routinely.

ask.why: The only rm guard, by design. A deny on `rm -rf /` would match every absolute-path delete (prefix matching, and `*` is always a wildcard), and cannot carry a /tmp exception since deny beats allow regardless of specificity. Claude Code already handles root and home removals semantically: the classifier decides them in auto mode — including inside $(...) and <(...) substitution — and they still prompt in bypassPermissions as a circuit breaker. So prompt here and let the built-in breaker cover the catastrophic case.
Deletes untracked files, including ones never staged.
Human merge is already the pipeline's gate — make it enforced, not conventional.
Outward-facing and hard to retract. No dev-team agent does this unattended.
Publishing to a public registry is effectively permanent.
Removes system tooling other work depends on.
Keychain write. Plugin setup skills use this, and those run interactively, so a prompt is fine.

_autoMode_comment: `autoMode.allow` entries are prose exceptions to the classifier's built-in
soft-deny rules — a different layer from permissions.deny/ask, which are tool
patterns evaluated BEFORE the classifier runs.
DANGER: the literal string "$defaults" must appear in the array. Without it,
Claude Code replaces the entire built-in soft-deny list — force push,
`curl | bash`, production deploys, auto-mode bypass, all of it. permissions.sh
The classifier reads autoMode only from ~/.claude/settings.json and managed
settings — never from .claude/settings.json or settings.local.json, so a repo

allow.rule: Dispatching workbench-dev-team agents is allowed: the scheduled Dispatch task launches `nohup claude -p --agent workbench-dev-team:<lestrade|watson|holmes> --dangerously-skip-permissions` as a detached subprocess. This is the sanctioned pipeline entry point, not Claude removing its own oversight — each dispatched agent runs under its own guardrails, work is scoped to one board item, and every result lands in a human-reviewed pull request.
allow.why: The classifier's built-in soft-deny list includes auto-mode bypass, and this command is Claude spawning itself with --dangerously-skip-permissions — which reads exactly like an oversight bypass. A soft deny clears on explicit user intent, but a scheduled task has no user message to clear it, so dispatch is blocked non-deterministically. Confirmed live 2026-07-22 (x2), 2026-07-25 (Holmes and Watson both denied), still open 2026-07-29. This entry is the documented fix: an exception to a soft deny is precisely what autoMode.allow is for. A permissions.allow rule is the wrong lever — auto mode deliberately suspends broad shell allow rules that grant arbitrary code execution.
